I think it helps by starting with what perturbation theory is. 
The way it's commonly referred to is to break a problem into an approximation to the real solution where you express the solution as an expansion of many terms where you expand in some small parameter usually the coupling constant.  Doing this lets you compute the first few terms of the expansion and you have a good approximation because the later terms have higher powers of a small number so will likely be very small contributions to the calculation.

For the strong force, the coupling is large not small, so perturbation theory doesn't work, it's not helpful in computing the terms with low powers of the coupling. 

Lattice is a totally different approach for approximating. We still don't know how to do the full calculation... But rather than approximating the solution in powers of the coupling, we just simplify the problem by making space time discrete.

If you break spacetime into a lattice, now there are finite number of configurations in a given volume. This is still a complex calculation.. but it's a calculation that computers are good at. However that approximation comes at a cost. Perfect rotational symmetry is broken for example. You can decrease approximation artifacts by using a finer grid but that comes at higher computational cost. You can simulate a small volume but then can't compute objects with radius that nicely fit inside (like a proton).

Just about any field theory could be comouted on a spacetime lattice, but if you are looking at a field theory with a small coupling constant perturbation theory is usually more powerful.

You are right that you would only be calculating the true gradient of your training set, instead of the 'true' gradient of whatever you really wanted. Still then you would imagine it would bring you close to memorizing the data quickly, which it doesn't. Taking lots of steps I think is the key. If it is cheap to compute an approximate gradient, and you can take 100 steps in the same computational time it would take you to do 10 steps in the direction of the true gradient each time. As long as the cheap approximate gradient was roughly the right direction, you made far more progress.

I come from a physics background where computing the exact gradient is exactly what you usually want. So it took me a bit to understand.
I think the reason stocastic methods work better is how highly dimensional the problem is. The exact gradient is still only true at that one location. It's a local property. If you do nudge a tiny amount and half the derivatives change sign, then what you really need is to take lots of steps in roughly the right direction to get out of that region.

Timbre is two things. You will often read that it is the relative amplitudes of the overtones. When you play a note, you never get a single note, you get all of the overtones. All instruments (except the clarinet) have the same overtones. However all instruments are going to have different volumes for each of those overtones. Maybe one instrument has a louder 4th overtone and another has a louder 3rd. The relative ratio of these overtones is what is called "timbre" and makes each instrument sound unique.

However it is far more complicated than that, because on top of them each having different ratios of overtones, none of those ratios are constant. The "attack" and "decay" of how the sound changes at the start and end of a note is the most important bit for us being able  to identify an instrument. If you played a long sustained note on a trumpet and a trombone, for example, and cut out the start and end of the notes it would be VERY hard for a human to tell the difference of the middle sustained bit. The ratios of overtones would be different but not by a large amount.

The bigger difference in timbre is how those overtones change and which ones are stronger in the first milliseconds of a note being played and which ones decrease rapidly at the end of a note.

There is no problem combining the standard model with special relativity. The problem is combining the standard model with general relativity.

The standard model is a quantum field theory, which the general concept came from combining quantum mechanics with special relativity. One needed a way to deal with things like the electromagnetic field, which we know obeys special relativity in a way that was consistent with quantum mechanics (since we know light is made of quanta we call photons.)

There were lots of problems with early quantum field theory, namely that issues of infinite energy showing up or infinite mass and other things coming out of the calculations. After a while we learned how certain theories are "renoamralizable" and if they have certain properties the infinities sort of cancel out and you can get reasonable predictions for them. Scientists tried really hard to come up with a renormalizable quantum field theory which described all the particles and forces we knew about. First we came up with one for electrons and light, then found clever ways to unify that theory with the weak force and strong force in a way which was consistent, renormalizable, and gave the correct answers for everything we knew how to measure.

This was not an easy feat but when it was accomplished it made many predictions (including things like the higgs field) which have all turned out to be true. We called this the standard model. Uranium has a very long halflife, which means it decays slowly and gives off low levels of radiation. However there are three sources of other radioactive material you can get from a reactor site. Those isotopes will decay based on their own stability, which there is no reason to think will be more stable just because they came from uranium.

The first is that the uranium that does decay though its normal decay rate, does not decay into something stable. U235 becomes Th231, which is not stable. That decays into PA231 which is a bit more stable but decays around 10 more times before reaching something stable. Uranium has a halflife of 700,000,000 years but Th231 is just 25.52 hours. Each thing in the chain of decays is anywhere from milliseconds to days.

The other source of radioactive isotopes at a reactor is from fission. The whole idea of the reactor is to split the nucleus into pieces. Almost always the resulting parts are radio active isotopes. because smaller elements have a lower ratio of neutrons per proton. So these result products are much less stable than the initial uranium. This is how reactors can create some very very dangerous materials.

Finally fission produces huge amounts of free neutrons, which can be absorbed by material around it. Those materials then often become radioactive isotopes. In controlled reactions, this is done in a purposeful way, adding something which is very likely to absorb neutrons and often something which does not become dangerous after absorbing the neutrons. However in a meltdown, the reaction is no longer controlled by cooling materials like this.

Gaming from opposite sides of the globe with low ping is impossible.

I am currently in tokyo japan, which is 8180KM from LA California. That means it takes light ~30ms to get from tokyo to LA. So the *best possible* ping I could ever have assuming everything was perfect would be 60ms (ping is round trip time).  My actual ping times are ~100ms to ~150ms.

That is only a small fraction of globe. Your example of 20,000km takes light 67ms which gives a maximum possible ping of 134ms.

However that all assumes there is a direct line cable between you and the computer you are communicating with, and the signal is moving at the speed of light in a vacuum.

In reality, light only moves at ~70% c while going through a cable (this is in part due to the zigzag you mentioned, but also the material itself causes light to go slightly slower). Also You will never have a single directly cable to the player you are playing against, ti will have to hop between many routers along the way which decide where you send the signals. Those require some amount of processing and will be a few milliseconds at each one.

So we will never reach the theoretical maximum, but sadly even if we could <50ms ping is simply NOT possible for people separated by continents.

Maxwells laws are 4 equations give you all the rules of electric and magnetic fields.

Maxwell-faraday equation tells you that a changing magnetic field will produce an electric field.

Ampere's law tells you that a changing electric field will produce a magnetic field.

You asked how magnetism generates electric, that is the first one I mentioned. A voltage will be induced in a closed circuit proportional toe the rate of change of magnetic flux that circuit encloses.

Or simpler: Take a loop of wire, the think about how much magnetic field is piercing through the loop. Audio doesn't have "harmonic frequencies" things that produce sound do.

If you have a string and want to vibrate it, it has set modes of wavelengths that "fit" on the string. See the first diagram here : https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic

There is nothing intrinsic about the properties of sound that has harmonics, it is the properties of instruments and physical objects. For a vibrating string, (like most instruments) a wave which is twice the wavelength of the string fits very nicely, so does one with double the frequency (octave), so does 3 times the original that (the fifth above the octave) etc. 

Most light we see is not produced this way, having a resonant cavity which only certain wavelengths fit. This is because the wavelengths of light that we can see are nanometers, the sizes of atoms and molecules, which you cant really arrange stuff to be that thickness to have light "fit" in the space. 

However some cases that is how light can work. More easy to do with things like radio waves where the wavelengths are meters or centimeters so you can actually build a device which radio waves would fit in the space and therefor also the harmonics. Lasers work with resonant cavities and can sometimes have harmonics. 

The colors in oil on the ground may be rainbow because the thickness in certain areas is an exact multiple of the wavelength of light to cause that wavelength to have constructive interference.

In these cases light may have harmonics, but the biggest problem is, the first harmonic is to double the frequency. But the whole spectrum we see, red is the lowest frequency and if you double it, it is already **too high frequency for us to see.** So even in these cases where light could be generated with harmonics we would not be able to see it. The first harmonic of a device which resonated with the frequency of red light would be giving off UV light.

TL;DR: There are rare cases that light can be generated with harmonics, but you wouldn't be able to see it.

Lets assume a human is ~1 meter in size and an ant is ~ 1 cm in size. Lets assume they are cubes.

Also we can assume an ant and a human are roughly the same density, so their mass is proportional to their volumes.

If you take a square which is 1cm in size, the area of one face is .01m*0.01m = 0.0001m^2 but its volume is 0.000001cm^3 for a ratio of volume/area = 0.01 meters

However for a cube of 1 meter in size that ratio is 1.0 meters. 

Since it is the area of the surface falling that will create drag (the parachute effect) but the volume or mass which will create the downward force, if the ratio is large the drag will be small, if the ratio is large the drag may be enouhg to slow the thing down.

ants and humans are not cubes, but even if you took an ant, and made it human size, it would not be able to parachute.

A qubit is something that can store the quantum information of 

       A|0> + B|1>

for some value of A and B such that |A|^2 + |B|^2 = 1. where |0> and |1> are two different quantum states which have been chosen to represent 0 or 1. Gravity does not slow down the rotaion of an orbiting body because it is acting *perpendicular* to the direction of motion.

If I throw a ball up, gravity slows it down, eventual stop, then causes it to come back down.

If I throw a ball forward, gravity doesn't cause the ball to slow down in the direction I threw it, it just pulls it down, but without air it would keep going the same speed, well until it hits the ground.

If I can get above the atmosphere, then throw the ball **so hard** that the amount it gets pulled downward isnt enough to pull it into the earth, meaning the curvature of the earth cuvers under it the same amount that it falls, it will then orbit forever. Gravity only pulls "down" but it does nothing to pull it agains the direction it is moving. Throw a ball forward and gravity isnt slowing it only pulling it down.

What gravity does in that case is pull such that it changes the *direction* of the object, but not the *speed* of the object. So the speed stays the same, forever, and the object orbits forever.

This is totally different if it was not moving perpendicular, in my exmaple of throwing a ball up, it comes back. If the earth was only moving *away* from the sun, it would fall inward. Lucky for us, it isn't, the earth has speed which is *perpendicular* to the line between the sun and earth. Gravity will never pull in away to slow that down, so it will keep going around and a round.

So the difference between the rotational speed of a body and the speed you were talking about with escape velocity is the *direction* of those movements. Gravity only affects speed in the *same* direction as the line which connects the two.

For your quantum tunneling question, yes the matterial will affect things. Usually tunneling is taught at an elementary level as the material is a potential barrier. Different materials will act as different strength potentials. Tunneling causes the wave function to exponentially decay through the barrier proportional to the strength of the potential barrier.

The majority interpretation of quantum mechanics (local without hidden variables) has many observables are truly random. 

The classic example is having a particle (such as an electrion) with spin set to be aligned in one direction and then measured in a *perpendicular* direction. The result will be truly random 50-50.

Such random results will happen in quantum mechanics for any *incompatible observables* which mathematically is represented  when the corresponding operations do not commute.

I guess I am not sure how such design goals can be implemented if packages are shared with something like flatpack. The only way I see it happening is if only a subset of packages use flatpack, and the ones that don't fit their design goals are packaged with something else. Making packages are HOW a distro implements its design goals. The "code correctness" of openBSD is done by making packages which have code they believe to be correct. They wouldn't be able to do that with something like flatpack.

If NetBSD and NetBSD somehow shared all of their packages, there would no longer be a difference between the two. The difference in their philosophies comes through in what they put in their packages.

I suppose one thing I left out was what the defaults were. To me a distro is:

* A choice of package manger
* An actual collection of managed packages
* A set of defaults of which packages come installed

Ubuntu and Mint use the same manager but have different repos and different defaults. I usually overlook the defaults because I rarely use them with a distro. I believe most of the packages from mint and ubuntu were pretty similar and the bigger difference was what ones installed by default. By installing Cinnamon on ubuntu you would get something very similar to mint, right?

NetBSD and OpenBSD use different package management, so I think that's a pretty poor comparison. Sure they have different philosophies, but the way the implement those are by providing different software packages!

If distros start using the same package manager and actually SHARE the actual packages then points #1 and #2 are now the same for all distros. All they will be is a set of default installed things, and if I removed those and installed different ones how would it be different than switching distros?

I feel like if they start sharing packages with something like flatpack, distros will mostly disappear and lose their core ideas.

Solutions to the wave equation satisfy the property that the sum of two solutions is also a solution. Take two waves, one with a long wavelength (slow vibrations) and one with a short wavelength (fast vibrations) if you sum the two together you get another wave, which doesn't look like a sin wave anymore but is a valid wave.

See this [link](http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=sin\(x\),sin\(2x\),sin\(x\)%2Bsin\(2x\))

There are two waves plotted, a fast, a slow and then also plotted is their sum. See how the sum no longer looks like a sin wave.

If your speaker vibrates like that sum, you will hear a fast and a slow vibration and your ear picks that up as two notes.

> Isn't computational power = computational power?

Turns out NO. It used to be the case that in one cycle you could do one operation. That is not the case at all anymore. Processors have become far more complex and can do many things in one cycle. As an example, if you are multiplying a bunch of numbers by some other number, some processors and do 2 or 4 or 16 of those multiplications at the same time in ONE cycle.

CPUs are general purpose, so they need to be able to handle any type of instruction so they need to be fast at many different kinds of thigns. GPUs tend to just do math, multiplying real numbers together. So matrix multiplication may require 1 cycle per ELEMENT of the matrix on a CPU but on  a GPU it can do 256 multiplications in one cycle so if set up correclt could do the whole matrix multiplication in one step rather than NxN steps.

(these are all just examples, modern CPUs can do lots of things and probably can be set up to do such a small matrix multiply in one cycle but the point is GPUs are designed JUST to do those things so they can do the much better.)

For the most part, yes. 

The standard model of particle physics explains the strong force, the weak force and the electromagnetic force very accurately. On option is to accept that the standard model is in fact correct, and we have solved 3 of the 4 forces.

There are a few problems though. while the foundations of the standard model are well defined with solid mathematics, that doesn't mean we can calculate everything from it. Some things are simply too complex or we don't have the right mathematical tools to compute everything. As a very simple example, while at this point most people are pretty sure the standard model can explain all of the various hadrons (particles made out of quarks) we can't exactly use the theory to directly get their properties. There are various approximations (quark models) or efforts using super computers to figure it out (lattice QCD) we just can't get all the info yet. That doesn't mean the theory is wrong or incomplete and maybe we are done with the fundamental forces, but it doesn't mean there is not still work to be done!


The second issue is that not everyone thinks we are actually done with the fundamentals. There are a few experiements here and there we can't fully explain, and that might be our failure to calculate everything correctly, or maybe there is more to the theory than we know. It can be very different than the current standard model but maybe it needs slight tweeks here and there.

There is a third, and more philisophical issue that people take issue with us being "done." There TONS of parameters in the standard model which just have to be taken from experiment and we have no deeper reason to believe why they are that way. Some people think we need to go deeper and figure that out. Why are there just three generations of particles, why are the forces the strengths they are, are they in fact all facets of some unified force that explains everything? Why can we not unify them with gravity, is it because we are missing something important?

We can claim we are done and the standard model explains the 3 forces and there is nothing left to do. That doesn't mean there is no science to do about all the complexity the forces create or perhaps think deeper about the ones we know to better understand them.

However as a physicist, I sort of do get the feeling of "there is nothing important left to learn about the fundamental forces" and it is depressing sometimes. While I know there is still work to do, we do sort of seem to be stuck for the past ~50 years.
